title: Flatness lifts from a nilpotent quotient with injective ideal multiplication
statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $I\subseteq R$ an ideal with $I^n=0$ for some integer $n\geq1$. Let $M$ be an $R$-module, and let $IM$ be the submodule generated by the products $am$ with $a\in I$, $m\in M$. Use module tensor products [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product] and flat modules [def-weil-pbc-flat-ring-map]. Suppose $M/IM$ is flat over $R/I$ and the multiplication map $\mu:I\otimes_R M\to M$, $a\otimes m\mapsto am$, is injective. Then $M$ is flat over $R$. No finite-generation or Noetherian hypothesis is imposed.

source.place: Tag 051C, lemma-what-does-it-mean, final assertion, with Tag 00M6, remark-Tor-ring-mod-ideal, identifying the Tor vanishing with injectivity of ideal multiplication.

proof.text: Compute $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(R,M)=0$ using the free resolution with $R$ in degree zero and zero in positive degrees. Apply the low-degree Tor sequence to $0\to I\to R\to R/I\to0$. Its boundary $\delta:\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(R/I,M)\to I\otimes_R M$ is injective, since its kernel is the image of the zero module $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(R,M)$. Its image is the kernel of $I\otimes_R M\to R\otimes_R M$. Under $R\otimes_R M\cong M$, $r\otimes m\mapsto rm$, this map is exactly $\mu$. The assumed injectivity of $\mu$ makes the image zero; hence $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(R/I,M)=0$.

source.place: Tag 051C, lemma-what-does-it-mean, proof of (2) and final assertion; the initial ideal sequence is the computation of Tag 00M6, remark-Tor-ring-mod-ideal.

proof.text: Let $N$ be any $R$-module with $IN=0$, and give it its $R/I$-module structure by $\bar r x=rx$. Take $F=(R/I)^{(N)}$ and the surjection $F\to N$ sending the basis vector indexed by $x$ to $x$; put $K=\ker(F\to N)$. Both $K$ and $F$ are killed by $I$. The free-restriction Tor bound, with $A=R$, $B=R/I$, $j=1$, and the basis set equal to the underlying set of $N$, gives $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(F,M)=0$ by Step 1. The low-degree Tor sequence of $0\to K\to F\to N\to0$ therefore gives an injection $\delta_N:\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(N,M)\to K\otimes_R M$ whose image is the kernel of $K\otimes_R M\to F\otimes_R M$.

source.place: Tag 051C, lemma-what-does-it-mean, proof of (2) and final assertion; the initial ideal sequence is the computation of Tag 00M6, remark-Tor-ring-mod-ideal.

proof.text: By the natural quotient-ring tensor isomorphisms, the last tensor map in Step 2 identifies with $K\otimes_{R/I}(M/IM)\to F\otimes_{R/I}(M/IM)$. Naturality applies to the inclusion $K\to F$, so this is an identification of maps, not just of objects. Flatness of $M/IM$ over $R/I$ makes this map injective. Thus the boundary in Step 2 has zero image; its injectivity gives $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(N,M)=0$ for every $N$ killed by $I$.

source.place: Tag 051C, lemma-what-does-it-mean, proof of (2) and final assertion; the initial ideal sequence is the computation of Tag 00M6, remark-Tor-ring-mod-ideal.

proof.text: Induct on $m\geq1$ to show $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(N,M)=0$ for every $N$ with $I^mN=0$. The case $m=1$ is Step 3. For $m\geq2$, use $0\to IN\to N\to N/IN\to0$. Here $I^{m-1}(IN)=I^mN=0$ (expand products of ideal generators), and $I(N/IN)=0$ because every product $ax$ with $a\in I$ belongs to $IN$. Induction kills $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(IN,M)$, and Step 3 kills $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(N/IN,M)$. Exactness of the three-term degree-one Tor segment now says the kernel of the map from $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(N,M)$ to the zero module is the image of the zero module. Consequently $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(N,M)=0$.

source.place: Tag 051C, lemma-what-does-it-mean, proof of (2) and final assertion; the initial ideal sequence is the computation of Tag 00M6, remark-Tor-ring-mod-ideal.

proof.text: Take the exponent $n\geq1$ from the hypothesis $I^n=0$. Every $R$-module $N$ satisfies $I^nN=0$, so Step 4 gives $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(N,M)=0$ for all $N$. In particular, for every ideal $J\subseteq R$, this holds for $N=R/J$. Tor symmetry gives $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,R/J)=0$. The flat-Tor ideal criterion then proves that $M$ is flat over $R$.

theorem of_nilpotent_ideal_multiplication_injective
    {R : Type u} [CommRing R] (J : Ideal R)
    {M : Type v} [AddCommGroup M] [Module R M]
    (n : ℕ) (hn : 1 ≤ n) (hJ : J ^ n = ⊥)
    (hflat : Module.Flat (R ⧸ J) (M ⧸ J • (⊤ : Submodule R M)))
    (hinj : Function.Injective
      (TensorProduct.lift ((LinearMap.lsmul R M).comp J.subtype))) :
    Module.Flat R M
